cards.heading: Definition and the two-sided premise
cards.question: What are budget caps for autonomous agents, and what premise justifies sizing them per job rather than fixing them globally?
cards.answer: Operator-set hard limits on tokens, tool calls, re-check iterations, and wall-clock duration; sized per job because output degrades in both directions — too small cuts the agent off as a low-confidence stub, too large lets it wander, spend, and add noise.

cards.heading: Time-boxed and CI runs
cards.question: Which caps matter most for a time-boxed engagement or CI run, and why?
cards.answer: Wall-clock and iteration caps — the requirement is that the run always finishes inside a window, even if it finishes incomplete.

cards.heading: Deep single-target work
cards.question: Why does a deep investigation of a single target loosen the token cap rather than tighten it?
cards.answer: Because the value comes from the agent being able to abandon a hypothesis and re-plan — behaviour a tight token budget would foreclose.

cards.heading: Broad sweeps need per-target budgets
cards.question: Why does a broad sweep across many targets need per-target budgets instead of one pooled allowance?
cards.answer: A single target that turns into a rabbit hole would otherwise consume the entire run and starve every target after it.

cards.heading: Asymmetric failure modes
cards.question: Why is overbudgeting a harder error to notice than underbudgeting, and what operating rule follows from that?
cards.answer: Underbudgeting fails visibly as a legible low-confidence stub, while overbudgeting produces plausible extra output that costs money and dilutes genuine findings — so start tight and loosen only when real work is demonstrably being cut off.
